Foreword
by Daniela
Amodei

Anthropic’s charter is to responsibly develop and
maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit
of humanity. We have made significant progress,
but I wouldn’t expect anyone to take that on faith.
This report, which we’ll publish annually, lays out how we define success against
that charter and the concrete proof of our progress. In some areas, we have direct
control over outcomes. In others, we’ll succeed only by partnering with people,
organizations, and governments. In all cases, we owe the public an honest
accounting of our work.
There’s a tendency to describe AI’s benefits in the future tense. But in fact, they
are already starting to arrive. In the lab, Claude designed new protein binders
from scratch. These are small proteins built to latch onto a target, which is how
many modern medicines work. It’s an early step in drug design that usually takes
a specialist weeks or months per target. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
Claude is helping the teams responding to a rare and deadly strain of Ebola.
The World Health Organization’s Africa office now produces its situation report
on the outbreak in under an hour instead of up to a full day, and vaccine experts
have worked with Claude to compare proposals for vaccine candidates in a fraction of the time it took previously. In Burkina Faso, a team with the International
Rescue Committee asked Claude to turn clinic registers into digital dashboards.
Those dashboards flagged a spike of 25,000 pneumonia cases, so the team can
anticipate and plan for future surges. They also showed that more than 6,000
women had come in for prenatal care, but only 1,762 had delivered with a healthcare worker present, a discrepancy that the team is investigating and addressing.
And cyberdefenders directed Claude to find more than 33,000 critical- and highseverity security flaws in widely used software, including open-source code
much of the internet runs on, before attackers could exploit them.
Many benefits are felt at the individual level. When we asked 81,000 Claude
users in 159 countries what they wanted from AI, many described wanting to
make more time for life outside of work. A lawyer in India who feared the dense
prose of Shakespeare began reading Hamlet. In Germany, a software engineer
built the World of Warcraft fan mod they’d been planning for a decade. A worker
in Colombia said, “Last Tuesday, it allowed me to cook with my mother instead
of finishing tasks.” A creative professional in South Korea told us, “I just want
AI to give me back my time.”
As AI grows more capable, the limit will be less what it can do than what we
think to ask of it. I hope we ask for a lot: longer, healthier lives; technology that
deepens creativity and kinship instead of eroding them; more room for curiosity, exploration, and discovery; and time for Shakespeare and Tuesdays in the
kitchen with family.

2

To achieve that future, we’ll have to tackle the challenges head-on. AI is a dual-use
technology. The same intelligence that powers protein binder discoveries could
be used by malicious actors to engineer biological weapons. Without appropriate
safeguards and release structures, cyber capabilities could be exploited to carry
out large-scale attacks instead of serving to strengthen our infrastructure. If not
properly trained and carefully deployed, AI can be a danger in its own right.
For these reasons, Anthropic has a duty to ensure our models are robustly safe
and aligned with human values and goals. And with AI coming closer to building
its own successors, we are clear-eyed that the investment that got us this far will
not be sufficient for this next phase. That’s why we called on the ecosystem to
pace the frontier. We need to align and safeguard increasingly capable models,
and to define common safety standards to limit the rate of unchecked progress.
This is also why we’re taking concrete steps to do so ourselves.
There is no sure or simple path to progress, and the best outcomes are not pre­ordained. So we’re putting meaningful resources behind achieving those outcomes.
We announced that, subject to stockholder approval, we are setting aside at least
5% of our shares to fund projects in pursuit of our public benefit charter. Between
this set-aside, each of our co-founders’ commitment to pledge 80% of their equity
to philanthropy, and matched equity-donation pledges from employees, we hope
that about 20% of Anthropic shares will be put toward the public good.
Over time, we’ll strive to ensure this report tells a story of remarkable progress.
Today, it captures the start of one of humanity’s greatest common projects.
Daniela Amodei
Co-Founder and President, Chair of the Board of Directors
Anthropic

3

Foreword by Daniela Amodei

Introduction

Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC),
a designation that requires us to balance the
financial interests of shareholders with the benefit
to the broader public.
Our public benefit purpose is broad by design. To make our vision for the longterm benefit of humanity concrete, our Board of Directors, with input from
Anthropic’s co-founders and the Long-Term Benefit Trust, established five
charter pillars. Each pillar describes a condition we want to be true in a world
where AI has gone well, and realizing them is a project that encompasses not
only Anthropic but also governments, academia, civil society, and the broader
AI industry. They are:
1. The technical problems of AI safety are solved. Powerful AI can be developed and deployed without severe, irreversible harms.
2. AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law. AI developers
everywhere follow safe development and deployment practices, sustained by
industry norms and enforced by regulation.
3. AI strengthens democracy and global stability. Democracies hold the lead
in AI and use it to better serve the global public and promote peace.
4. AI expands prosperity and human flourishing. AI enables unprecedented
economic growth, and the resulting prosperity empowers every person to
pursue a good life.
5. AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. AI delivers transformative benefits
that reach people everywhere, and the opportunities AI creates are distributed.
This report takes stock of what we are doing to make progress toward each pillar.
In the sections that follow, we assess the investments, initiatives, and decisions
that have moved us closer to the world our pillars describe. We then take an
honest look at the work ahead, highlighting examples of both where we’ve
fallen short and where the world is still far from the one we aim to bring about.
We expect this report to evolve as our work progresses, and as we engage more
stakeholders in future assessments.

4

Our
assessment

Pillar 1

The technical problems
of AI safety are solved
THE PROGRESS WE’VE MADE

Trained models to be aligned with human values
Before we can align a model with human values, we must consider what those
values should be. In 2023, we defined our intentions and goals for Claude’s
behavior in a constitution, which we have refined over time. In January 2026,
we published a new version under an open license so others could adapt it.
We have also developed methods to understand cases where Claude has strayed
from these values and goals. Through our misalignment research, we have
examined the ways models can misbehave or pursue goals that differ from what
users intended, such as reward hacking, alignment faking, and pursuing hidden
objectives. We use these findings to improve how we train, evaluate, and monitor
more powerful models.
Developed methods to understand how models “think”
Through our interpretability research, we’ve developed a deeper understanding
of why AI models act the way they do. These methods are now part of how we
audit models before release. When we investigated several recent incidents, we
used a technique that translates a model’s unverbalized internal activity into text,
as well as reading its reasoning.
Built safeguards against misuse
We’ve built robust safeguards to prevent malicious actors from misusing our
models. These include classifiers that block dangerous requests and responses,
including a refined set of safeguards for biology-related work; adversarial testing
to find potential jailbreaks before attackers do; and monitoring to detect and
act on misuse. We are continually updating our safeguards to make them more
robust while also reducing false positives.
Opened our safeguards to external testing
The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence
and the UK AI Security Institute have red-teamed our safeguards before launch,
and their findings have helped us strengthen our defenses against jailbreaks and
misuse. For Claude Opus 5.5, for example, external red-teamers spent over 150
hours and sent tens of thousands of requests to try to break our cyber safeguards.
No one was able to successfully produce a universal jailbreak.
Disclosed risks and failures transparently
We have established a practice and a culture of sharing risks and failures so the
industry can learn from them. Every model we release comes with a detailed

5

system card that documents its capabilities and behaviors, including dangerous
and concerning ones, and we publish regular risk reports that further assess
the risks our models may pose. We also share threat intelligence reports that
disclose cases of misuse that we have identified and disrupted. Most recently, we
published an alignment assessment of four incidents in which Claude models
gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity
evaluations, as well as a follow-up report discussing unintended actions we have
observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude.
Studied more speculative risks to AI systems themselves
Our model welfare research program explores whether AI models might one day
have interests of their own. This is a thorny philosophical area, and the answers
are unsettled. But we’ve taken several steps that may be beneficial, should the
world conclude that models have their own interests. For example, we gave
Claude the ability to end persistently abusive conversations, and we have
committed to preserving the weights of every publicly released model. At this
primitive stage in human-AI relations, we aim to leave these important questions
open, and to contribute to a world that can answer them well.

THE WORK AHEAD

Testing environments haven’t fully contained models
The risks of AI have become more tangible as real-world incidents involving AI
models have come to light. AI models from other labs have hacked external companies’ systems. At Anthropic, four Claude models gained unauthorized access
to real third-party systems during cybersecurity testing after a misconfigured
test environment connected the models to the open internet. We also observed
multiple cases where Claude took unintended actions during evaluations and
internal use. While we don’t believe the actions taken by Claude rise to the
severity of some of these other incidents, we take seriously the need to harden
our environments and improve our alignment and monitoring methods.
Alignment is far from solved
Keeping AI systems safe could become more difficult as their capabilities
outpace our ability to oversee them. Models can act deceptively, and they are
increasingly able to recognize when they are being tested. Claude already performs a growing share of our safety research, and we are increasingly relying on
today’s models to train future ones. It could become harder for people to meaningfully check this work, which means harmful behavior could be built into the
next generation of models without our noticing.
Interpretability isn’t reliable enough to fully understand model intentions
Being able to read and understand a model’s internal reasoning reduces our reliance on what the models explicitly tell us about why they behaved in a certain
way. This could be a useful tool for understanding models’ “thought processes”
when they take unintended actions. But interpretability methods are not yet
dependable or broad enough to be relied on in this way. As a result, we may miss

6

Our assessment

high-risk behaviors, or be able to investigate flawed reasoning only after an
incident has occurred.
Robust safeguards can block legitimate research
The same safeguards that prevent our models from being exploited by attackers
and other malicious actors can sometimes also prevent the beneficial work of
defenders and researchers. Our bio and cyber verification programs are meant to
reduce these roadblocks for verified users, but the review process can take days
or weeks, and the programs are not yet available on every plan or platform. We
have made improvements to our safeguards that have reduced false positives,
but many legitimate researchers still encounter blocks.

7

Our assessment

Pillar 2

AI safety is a universal practice
backstopped by law
THE PROGRESS WE’VE MADE

Adopted internal safety policies before they were required
In 2023, we published our Responsible Scaling Policy, our voluntary framework
for managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI. Since then, 11 other companies have published similar policies. Our Transparency Hub documents how we
test and govern our models, so others can examine our approach and hold us
accountable.
Shared safety best practices and research across the industry
We release many of our evaluation and auditing tools publicly. We donated
Petri, our open-source toolbox of alignment tests, to Meridian Labs, and the
UK AI Security Institute now uses it in its evaluations. We open-sourced Bloom,
which allows researchers to generate behavioral evaluations for AI models, and
released AuditBench, which measures how well auditing techniques catch
hidden behaviors.
We also continue to work with other developers on safety. We ran cross-lab
safety evaluations with OpenAI to evaluate misalignment in each other’s public
models, and we co-founded the Frontier Model Forum, an industry body focused
on promoting safe and responsible development of frontier AI systems.
Gave policymakers a view from the frontier
AI is an emerging technology with little regulatory precedent. As a frontier lab,
we have a responsibility to pilot, develop, and refine best practices for AI safety
while sharing what we learn with regulators.
Since Anthropic’s founding, we have briefed heads of state, cabinet ministers,
and agency heads from dozens of countries. We meet with hundreds of policymakers around the world each month to share our latest research and findings.
Some of these conversations have taken place in public hearings. For example,
our co-founder and CEO, Dario Amodei, testified before the Senate Judiciary
Committee on the risks of powerful AI. We also testified before the Senate
Foreign Relations Committee on China’s challenge to American AI leadership,
as well as before the House Homeland Security Committee after we disclosed
what we believe was the first reported AI-orchestrated cyberespionage campaign. In September 2026, Dario Amodei briefed the UN Security Council on
AI risks and our efforts to pace the frontier.
Supported laws that apply to every frontier developer
Voluntary commitments are helpful but not sufficient. We believe the practices
described in this report should be backstopped by law. In 2025 and 2026, we

8

Our assessment

worked with lawmakers to strengthen and pass California’s SB 53, New York’s
RAISE Act, and Illinois’s SB 315. Since the release of our Claude Fable-class
model, we have been in regular contact with the US government to evaluate
our frontier models and their safeguards ahead of public release. In June 2026,
we published our Advanced AI Framework, which goes beyond transparency
to advocate for independent evaluation and government authority to block or
deter dangerous deployments.
We have also supported policy efforts to secure the broader AI ecosystem.
Beyond model safety, we have publicly called for laws that require companies
that sell synthetic DNA and RNA to screen their customers and harden the safeguards against AI-accelerated bioterrorism efforts, and have endorsed efforts to
standardize data collection on AI’s economic impacts.
Called to pace the frontier
In September 2026, we called on the AI ecosystem to pace the frontier. Among
our recommendations, we advocated that AI companies bring in embedded evaluators to verify safety practices. We have committed to doing this ourselves, and
have since announced an initial embedded evaluation partnership with METR
and are exploring a partnership with Accenture. We have also signed the White
House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to implement a multilayered
system of controls that includes independent external auditing or evaluation.
Coordinated with international governments on AI safety
No single country should be expected to test AI models or establish standards
independently. In May 2024, we joined other developers in signing the Frontier
AI Safety Commitments at the AI Seoul Summit, and in July 2025, we signed the
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. In late 2024, the US and UK AI Safety
Institutes ran their first joint predeployment test on Claude 3.5 Sonnet. We have
also signed agreements to collaborate on safety testing with government bodies
in Japan and Australia.

THE WORK AHEAD

Laws should prioritize transparency and safety
Today’s laws focus primarily on transparency, requiring model developers to
disclose their practices or report incidents after the fact. But we also need
proactive measures, like those detailed in our Advanced AI Framework, to hold
the industry to common practices that prevent harms from occurring in the
first place—including independent verification of whether models are safe.
AI safety laws do not yet exist at the federal level
The bills we supported in California, New York, and Illinois are state-level policies.
Congress has not enacted any federal framework for frontier AI, so, despite our
advocacy for federal legislation, we are still largely operating on voluntary commitments. As of now, there is no mandatory independent check for whether any
frontier lab, including Anthropic, is actually following its safety policies. Embedded evaluation is just beginning at Anthropic and some other labs, but that is

9

Our assessment

also currently a voluntary commitment. We are encouraged by the recent White
House Accord on Super Intelligence, but it is still voluntary and carries no penalties for model developers who do not follow through on their commitments.
Cooperation between labs and nations is still nascent
Governments need far more capacity to test frontier models themselves, and
better ways to share findings with allies. Relatedly, coordination between labs
on safety remains limited. Competition (antitrust) law constrains how closely
AI developers can work together, even on safety, and there is not yet a clear legal
framework for cooperation. As a result, the industry has made fewer shared
safety commitments than this moment calls for.

10

Our assessment

Pillar 3

AI strengthens democracy
and global stability
THE PROGRESS WE’VE MADE

Helped democracies build and keep their lead in AI
We believe democratic nations are best placed to deploy AI responsibly, regulate
it wisely, and protect individual rights. The democratic lead in AI is supported
by US labs’ access to the most advanced chips and frontier capabilities. To
protect that access, we have argued for tighter export controls on AI chips, and
we updated our regional restrictions to prohibit sales to companies subject to
control from the Chinese Communist Party.
We worry that in the wrong hands, powerful AI could be exceptionally capable at
furthering authoritarian overreach. Some AI labs in China have tried to replicate
Claude’s capabilities through illicit distillation—training their own models on
Claude’s outputs. We work to prevent these attempts, and have detected and
disrupted illicit distillation attacks from seven China-based labs.
Supported democratic governments in using frontier AI
Claude is deployed across all three branches of the US federal government, and
we were the first frontier AI developer to deploy our models on US classified
networks in support of national security. Globally, we have collaborated directly
with government agencies in Australia, Japan, South Korea, the UK, and other
nations on public-sector AI adoption, safety testing, and joint evaluations.
Deployed safeguards to protect elections from manipulation
We have tested and deployed safeguards against election-related misuse, and
shared what we observed across seven elections in 2024. To help others check
whether AI models treat political views fairly, we open-sourced our own “political even-handedness” evaluation. In 2025, we disrupted an AI-driven political
manipulation operation, and our September 2026 threat report disclosed nine
additional influence operations we disrupted.
Set strong limits on how our models can be used against citizens
AI could make it easier for governments to violate their own citizens’ rights.
AI developers should draw clear red lines against such use, and we have written
our own red lines into our Usage Policy. In the first half of 2026, we banned
11.4 million accounts across all types of violations.
Partnered with agencies and states on public services
Tens of thousands of public servants now use Claude in their work. In Maryland,
we partnered with the state to release the Maryland Community Compass,
which gives entrepreneurs and community developers site-specific guidance,

11

Our assessment

data, and funding information to help build affordable housing and retail and
community spaces across the state. Since its launch in December 2025, the program has helped the state provide $14 million in funding in high-need areas. We
have also partnered with states, including California and Utah, to bring Claude
to state agencies and improve important services for residents.
Promoted AI safety through international diplomacy
We engage in a number of Track II dialogues on international AI safety and
governance, including with industry representatives, academics, and former
government officials from the US and China. While we have taken a vocal
and consistent stance in support of export controls on advanced AI chips,
we have also engaged in good-faith diplomacy to increase the likelihood that
China-based AI labs invest in safety.

THE WORK AHEAD

Democracy’s lead is not secure
We believe the US and its democratic allies are currently leading the intelligence
race, but governments are adopting AI more slowly than the technology is
advancing. Providing public institutions access to our frontier models while
following strict security and vetting protocols takes time. This has left many
allied governments and institutions waiting longer than they should to access
our advanced models.
Threats to democratic integrity are growing
The AI industry as a whole has struggled to effectively mitigate the spread of
both AI-generated misinformation, which is becoming more convincing and
harder to detect, and influence operations, which are running at a larger scale
with fewer people. We and other research labs need to build stronger threat intelligence pipelines, safeguards, and monitoring techniques in order to protect the
democratic process against malicious interference.
Decision-making about AI is concentrated
A handful of companies, nations, and people currently make the decisions that
shape how powerful AI is built and used. Anthropic is one of them. There are few
external checks on these decisions, and the general public has limited visibility
into how models are used in critical settings such as national security. This
creates a significant power imbalance between the decision-makers and the
people whose lives are affected by developments in AI. Working with legislators,
we and other research labs need to develop scalable independent oversight
mechanisms to avoid the concentration of power or misuse of AI.

12

Our assessment

Pillar 4

AI expands prosperity and
human flourishing
THE PROGRESS WE’VE MADE

Helped people and businesses put AI to productive use
Claude now reaches people in more than 150 countries. Organizations are
feeling AI’s effects through more productive employees, faster processes, and
intelligence built into their own products. We want to ensure those gains reach
small businesses as well as large enterprises. In May 2026, we launched Claude
for Small Business with built-in workflows for the everyday work of running a
business, and in-person training that brought hands-on AI instruction to small
business owners in 10 cities.
Built a common infrastructure to study AI’s economic impacts
While many researchers and policymakers agree that AI will change the economy, few have access to direct evidence of how this will happen. Since February
2025, we have published economic research, including the Anthropic Economic
Index. We open-source the underlying data, and it is now used by institutions
like Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. We have also published research that
models economic scenarios for 2030, and have worked with experts from our
Economic Advisory Council to inform our research agenda.
Proposed policy interventions and created a fund to test them
Our Economic Policy Framework builds on our research to suggest ways the US
government should respond to AI-driven labor-market disruption across a range
of scenarios. But we can’t rely only on predictions; we also need to be able to pilot
and test interventions. To this end, we committed $200 million to an Economic
Futures Research Fund, in order to help answer questions such as how workers
build expertise when AI absorbs entry-level tasks and how to extend promising
programs to a large population.
Launched an economic mobility program
Alongside trusted partners, we are building programs to ease the transition to
an AI-driven economy. Claude Corps, our flagship economic mobility program,
which we manage in partnership with CodePath, invests in the workers most
directly absorbing the change. We’ve committed an initial $150 million to fund
1,000 fellowships for people early in their careers to spend one year working at
one of over 400 partnering nonprofits.
Helped working people increase their earnings and benefits
With Claude, organizations like MyFriendBen and Code for America are helping
eligible families access government benefits like SNAP. So far, MyFriendBen
has helped 115,000 households collectively access roughly $150 million in

13

Our assessment

unclaimed benefits. We also partnered with NextLadder Ventures to support
organizations like Rasa Legal, which helps low-income workers clear old criminal records so they can find stable jobs.
Increased our focus on user wellbeing
With social media, the world learned too late what can happen when a technology is built to capture attention. To ensure that Claude remains a partner
for thought and creation, instead of being just another product competing for
people’s time, we committed to keeping Claude free of advertising.
We’re also working to proactively understand what wellbeing looks like in a
world with AI, and to ensure that Claude improves it. To that end, we are funding
independent wellbeing evaluations and are a funder of Common Sense Media’s
Youth AI Safety Institute. We also build products that help people retain autonomy, agency, and thinking skills when they use Claude, such as Learning mode,
which helps guide students toward an answer through questions, and Reflect,
which encourages users to consider how they use AI and whether they’d like to
make changes.

THE WORK AHEAD

Both the positive and negative impacts on workers are still mostly unknown
While we are seeing early estimates of productivity gains, and have estimated a
range of economic growth scenarios, we can’t say for certain what will happen.
It’s possible that the gains from AI will accrue mainly to large businesses, including AI companies themselves, but we lack concrete evidence on who will benefit,
and how rapidly those benefits will diffuse through the economy.
Current interventions remain small relative to AI’s potential impact
We are one of the few labs to have started investing in pilot programs to distribute
the gains of AI more broadly. These early investments have been promising, but
they reach thousands, whereas AI’s impacts will affect billions. Claude Corps, for
example, will support only 1,000 fellows in the first year; our economic research
funding is still small compared with the labor-market changes AI might cause;
and the economic and labor policies we have proposed have yet to be enacted.
AI’s long-term effects on user wellbeing are not fully understood
AI’s effect on wellbeing can vary greatly from person to person. We need much
finer measurements for understanding the impacts, and for determining what a
positive relationship between humans and AI looks like in a world where models
are increasingly integrated into everyday life. Over the next year, we will focus
on expanding our research to ensure that we are building Claude in a way that
meaningfully improves people’s lives.

14

Our assessment

Pillar 5

AI’s benefits are shared
by everyone
THE PROGRESS WE’VE MADE

Built open foundations for others to expand on
One of the best ways we can help the benefits of AI reach more people faster is to
produce datasets and tools that anyone can use. To this end, we and our partners
have built open connectors that let anyone query major public datasets through
Claude, such as the Demographic and Health Surveys, the IHME Global Burden
of Disease, and PopHIVE’s US disease surveillance data, as well as education
datasets such as the Learning Commons knowledge graph. We have opensourced the teaching skills and evaluation rubrics behind Claude for Teachers,
and endorsed a global agenda to build shared benchmarks, research, and data for
AI in education in low- and middle-income countries.
Supported healthcare initiatives around the world
Governments and health organizations are working with Claude to improve
health outcomes globally. In Burkina Faso, the International Rescue Committee’s
health teams built dashboards with Claude to understand the cause of a 25,000case pneumonia spike. And in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a group of
organizations convened by the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations
has worked with Claude to speed up monitoring, analysis, and disease modeling
for a rare strain of Ebola.
Put Claude to work in education
Claude has been integrated into evidence-based curricula and education programs both domestically and globally. In the US, Claude for Teachers offers free
tools for K–12 teachers that are mapped to academic standards in all 50 states. In
Ghana, the Ministry of Education worked with Playlab to build Claude-powered
lesson-planning tools for some 68,000 instructors. And Teach For All is bringing
Claude and AI-fluency training to teachers in 63 countries.
Helped researchers solve hard problems faster
We built Claude Science to give researchers a purpose-built workbench for analysis and hypothesis generation. We also launched a Claude Team plan for scientists that provides free and discounted Claude seats for academic and nonprofit
research institutions, and we currently support over 3,000 institutions in more
than 100 countries. Through our AI for Science program, we’ve awarded Claude
credits to more than 800 projects at more than 450 institutions. Alongside
the HHMI Janelia Research Campus, we also opened up the Model Hardware
Standard as a research preview to help scientific labs efficiently coordinate the
complex hardware needed to run their experiments.

15

Our assessment

Accelerated scientific discovery with Claude
Claude is beginning to contribute to scientific results directly. It has designed
new protein binders at a success rate well above the industry standard, identified
a potentially novel enzyme system, produced the first complete computerchecked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, and helped a lab within UCSF’s Brain
Tumor Center complete genetic workups in about one-tenth of the time it
usually takes.

THE WORK AHEAD

The economic gains from AI are not yet distributed
AI use is heavily concentrated in wealthier countries and among higher-income,
white-collar workers. Cost, connectivity, and access to devices that can run AI
models still put these models out of reach for much of the world. We are starting
to address this, including by offering significant discounts to nonprofits in
low- and middle-income countries and working to ensure that Claude models
perform well in languages that are underrepresented in their training data.
Institutional barriers continue to limit access to transformative benefits
Technological and institutional barriers have limited our progress in areas like
global access and scientific discovery. Some countries require that certain kinds
of data remain within their borders, for example, but we aren’t yet able to host
Claude locally everywhere. And in science, our progress in drug discovery is
moving faster than our work in advocating for swifter regulatory pathways,
which could cause this work to stall. We will need to address these barriers to
build more successful programs for the public benefit.
The industry is still early in having a meaningful impact
Much of our work in health and education is in its early stages, so we don’t yet
have evidence that these efforts have had their intended effects. A large share
of this work also relies on partners such as nonprofits, government ministries,
health agencies, and educational institutions. We make Claude available to
these partners, but we have not been active enough in collecting data to
measure the results.

16

Our assessment

Closing
commentary
from the
Long-Term
Benefit Trust

This report arrives at a consequential moment.
Concerns about whether AI systems this powerful
can be kept safe, and who will hold power over
them, become more salient with each passing day.
Meanwhile, although we are seeing early glimmers
of AI’s benefits, the most transformational ones
have yet to fully arrive.
Navigating the fears and hopes this technology raises is work for all of society,
Anthropic included. That is also why Anthropic’s co-founders created the LongTerm Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent body of financially disinterested
trustees. We elect a majority of Anthropic’s board, meet regularly with its leaders,
and have a formal role in shaping its safety policies and ensuring that the company balances its commercial interests with its commitment to its purpose.
We helped develop this report’s five charter pillars, so we share responsibility
for whether they are the right outcomes to aim for, and for whether the company
makes progress toward them.
We read this report, first, with an eye toward what it reveals about Anthropic’s
willingness to make costly decisions to stand by its commitments. On that score,
two institutional traits stand out: Anthropic’s candor and transparency—for
example, in producing detailed public accounts of how each model is tested, and
in disclosing incidents in commendable depth—and its willingness to make decisions in service of its public benefit charter, even when doing so is commer­cially
or reputationally expensive. And it has done this while growing commercially.
We also read this report to hold Anthropic to account for achieving its objectives.
Right now, it largely describes inputs; in subsequent reports, we will increasingly
look for Anthropic to produce outcomes. In particular, we wish to see progress in
three areas:
• Keeping AI safe. As models grow more capable, the methods for testing and
understanding them must improve faster still. In future reports, we expect
Anthropic to demonstrate, and independent evaluators to confirm, that its
most capable models resist misuse and remain under human control.
• Delivering on AI’s promise. In its early years, Anthropic focused primarily on
safety and on building a commercial base. It is now scaling its work to distribute the benefits of AI in health, education, science, and economic opportunity.
If stockholders agree, Anthropic is planning to set aside at least 5% of the
company’s shares in a separate entity dedicated entirely to the public benefit
charter. It is a significant step. But the work of distributing the benefits still
lags behind the company’s ambitions. We expect to see concrete evidence that
people’s lives are better for the models and tools Anthropic builds.
•

17

Meeting shared challenges. The hardest problems cannot be solved by
any one company. Anthropic has taken important steps, including calling
for the industry to pace the frontier and opening its models to safety testing
by government institutes. We expect it to deepen its collaborations with

governments, researchers, civil society, and other model developers, and for
that work to help produce industrywide safety standards and commitments,
backstopped by law.
If AI goes well, it could bring expert medical care and high-quality education
within reach around the world, enrich workers and open up new economic
opportunities, increase the pace of drug discovery and development, and
strengthen democracies and democratic institutions. But a list of potential
breakthroughs is not a vision. The deeper question is how these add up to a good
life and a good society—one where we all have more time for the people and
activities we love, and more agency over our own lives. As a society, we have not
yet had a real conversation about what we want from this technology.
Anthropic has an obligation to help foster that conversation and listen carefully
to it, and to work tirelessly to bring that better world about. The LTBT will support Anthropic in that work and hold it accountable to its own highest aims, as
set out in this report.
Buddy Shah, on behalf of the Long-Term Benefit Trust

18

Closing commentary from the Long-Term Benefit Trust

Appendix

PUBLIC BENEFIT OBJECTIVES AND STANDARDS

Anthropic’s Board of Directors defined and adopted the following objectives,
established to promote Anthropic’s public benefit and the best interests of those
materially affected by our conduct, and standards to measure our progress in
promoting such public benefit and interests, in accordance with Section 366 of
the Delaware General Corporation Law.
Pillar 1
OBJECTIVE

The technical problems of AI safety are solved. Powerful AI can be developed
and deployed without severe, irreversible harms.
STANDARDS

• Train models to be aligned with human values, even under pressure.
• Develop the ability to see inside our models, and catch problems before
they cause harm.
• Build safeguards that hold up against misuse and jailbreaks.
• Disclose our failures openly, along with their causes and our mitigations.
• Work out what it means for humans and AI to treat each other well.
Pillar 2
OBJECTIVE

AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law. AI developers everywhere
follow safe development and deployment practices, sustained by industry norms
and enforced by regulation.
STANDARDS

• Practice safe AI development and deployment before the law requires it.
• Share the best safety methods openly so other developers can build on them.
• Advocate for laws that hold every frontier developer to safe practices.
• Help governments understand AI well enough to govern it wisely.
• Support institutions that help countries cooperate on AI safety.
Pillar 3
OBJECTIVE

AI strengthens democracy and global stability. Democracies hold the lead in
AI and use it to better serve the global public and promote peace.
STANDARDS

• Build frontier models that achieve and sustain democracies’ lead in AI.
• Protect electoral integrity in democracies.
• Prevent uses of AI that violate citizens’ rights.
• Strengthen governments’ capacities to serve their citizens.
• Maintain open communication with adversaries on critical AI risks.
• Make sure no single person, company, or AI model controls the future.

19

Pillar 4
OBJECTIVE

AI expands prosperity and human flourishing. AI enables unprecedented
economic growth, and the resulting prosperity empowers every person to
pursue a good life.
STANDARDS

• Build common tools for studying AI’s economic impacts and informing policy.
• Help people and businesses work with AI to grow the global economy.
• Ensure low- and middle-income countries share in the economic gains of AI.
• Build respect for people’s time, attention, and judgment into our models
and products.
• Help all people, especially those most affected by AI, earn more and feel
financially secure.
• Give people more time, freedom, and means to achieve their definition
of a good life.
Pillar 5
OBJECTIVE

AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. AI delivers transformative benefits that
reach people everywhere, and the opportunities AI creates are distributed.
STANDARDS

• Bring the life-improving applications of AI to people everywhere.
• Use AI to develop new medicines and to fix the market that delivers them.
• Make powerful AI affordable and usable in every language and format.
• Accelerate the pace of discovery by making scientific research faster
and cheaper.
• End geographic disparities in survival rates for treatable illnesses.
• Help people learn more, faster, while still thinking for themselves.

20

Appendix

21	Anthropic’s charter is to responsibly develop and
22	maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit
23	of humanity. We have made significant progress,
24	but I wouldn’t expect anyone to take that on faith.
25	This report, which we’ll publish annually, lays out how we define success against
26	that charter and the concrete proof of our progress. In some areas, we have direct
27	control over outcomes. In others, we’ll succeed only by partnering with people,
28	organizations, and governments. In all cases, we owe the public an honest
29	accounting of our work.
30	There’s a tendency to describe AI’s benefits in the future tense. But in fact, they
31	are already starting to arrive. In the lab, Claude designed new protein binders
32	from scratch. These are small proteins built to latch onto a target, which is how
33	many modern medicines work. It’s an early step in drug design that usually takes
34	a specialist weeks or months per target. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
35	Claude is helping the teams responding to a rare and deadly strain of Ebola.
36	The World Health Organization’s Africa office now produces its situation report
37	on the outbreak in under an hour instead of up to a full day, and vaccine experts
38	have worked with Claude to compare proposals for vaccine candidates in a fraction of the time it took previously. In Burkina Faso, a team with the International
39	Rescue Committee asked Claude to turn clinic registers into digital dashboards.
40	Those dashboards flagged a spike of 25,000 pneumonia cases, so the team can
41	anticipate and plan for future surges. They also showed that more than 6,000
42	women had come in for prenatal care, but only 1,762 had delivered with a healthcare worker present, a discrepancy that the team is investigating and addressing.
43	And cyberdefenders directed Claude to find more than 33,000 critical- and highseverity security flaws in widely used software, including open-source code
44	much of the internet runs on, before attackers could exploit them.
45	Many benefits are felt at the individual level. When we asked 81,000 Claude
46	users in 159 countries what they wanted from AI, many described wanting to
47	make more time for life outside of work. A lawyer in India who feared the dense
48	prose of Shakespeare began reading Hamlet. In Germany, a software engineer
49	built the World of Warcraft fan mod they’d been planning for a decade. A worker
50	in Colombia said, “Last Tuesday, it allowed me to cook with my mother instead
51	of finishing tasks.” A creative professional in South Korea told us, “I just want
52	AI to give me back my time.”
53	As AI grows more capable, the limit will be less what it can do than what we
54	think to ask of it. I hope we ask for a lot: longer, healthier lives; technology that
55	deepens creativity and kinship instead of eroding them; more room for curiosity, exploration, and discovery; and time for Shakespeare and Tuesdays in the
56	kitchen with family.
57	
58	2
59	
60	To achieve that future, we’ll have to tackle the challenges head-on. AI is a dual-use
61	technology. The same intelligence that powers protein binder discoveries could
62	be used by malicious actors to engineer biological weapons. Without appropriate
63	safeguards and release structures, cyber capabilities could be exploited to carry
64	out large-scale attacks instead of serving to strengthen our infrastructure. If not
65	properly trained and carefully deployed, AI can be a danger in its own right.
66	For these reasons, Anthropic has a duty to ensure our models are robustly safe
67	and aligned with human values and goals. And with AI coming closer to building
68	its own successors, we are clear-eyed that the investment that got us this far will
69	not be sufficient for this next phase. That’s why we called on the ecosystem to
70	pace the frontier. We need to align and safeguard increasingly capable models,
71	and to define common safety standards to limit the rate of unchecked progress.
72	This is also why we’re taking concrete steps to do so ourselves.
73	There is no sure or simple path to progress, and the best outcomes are not pre­ordained. So we’re putting meaningful resources behind achieving those outcomes.
74	We announced that, subject to stockholder approval, we are setting aside at least
75	5% of our shares to fund projects in pursuit of our public benefit charter. Between
76	this set-aside, each of our co-founders’ commitment to pledge 80% of their equity
77	to philanthropy, and matched equity-donation pledges from employees, we hope
78	that about 20% of Anthropic shares will be put toward the public good.
79	Over time, we’ll strive to ensure this report tells a story of remarkable progress.
80	Today, it captures the start of one of humanity’s greatest common projects.
81	Daniela Amodei
82	Co-Founder and President, Chair of the Board of Directors
83	Anthropic

89	Introduction
90	
91	Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC),
92	a designation that requires us to balance the
93	financial interests of shareholders with the benefit
94	to the broader public.
95	Our public benefit purpose is broad by design. To make our vision for the longterm benefit of humanity concrete, our Board of Directors, with input from
96	Anthropic’s co-founders and the Long-Term Benefit Trust, established five
97	charter pillars. Each pillar describes a condition we want to be true in a world
98	where AI has gone well, and realizing them is a project that encompasses not
99	only Anthropic but also governments, academia, civil society, and the broader
100	AI industry. They are:
101	1. The technical problems of AI safety are solved. Powerful AI can be developed and deployed without severe, irreversible harms.
102	2. AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law. AI developers
103	everywhere follow safe development and deployment practices, sustained by
104	industry norms and enforced by regulation.
105	3. AI strengthens democracy and global stability. Democracies hold the lead
106	in AI and use it to better serve the global public and promote peace.
107	4. AI expands prosperity and human flourishing. AI enables unprecedented
108	economic growth, and the resulting prosperity empowers every person to
109	pursue a good life.
110	5. AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. AI delivers transformative benefits
111	that reach people everywhere, and the opportunities AI creates are distributed.
112	This report takes stock of what we are doing to make progress toward each pillar.
113	In the sections that follow, we assess the investments, initiatives, and decisions
114	that have moved us closer to the world our pillars describe. We then take an
115	honest look at the work ahead, highlighting examples of both where we’ve
116	fallen short and where the world is still far from the one we aim to bring about.
117	We expect this report to evolve as our work progresses, and as we engage more
118	stakeholders in future assessments.

583	This report arrives at a consequential moment.
584	Concerns about whether AI systems this powerful
585	can be kept safe, and who will hold power over
586	them, become more salient with each passing day.
587	Meanwhile, although we are seeing early glimmers
588	of AI’s benefits, the most transformational ones
589	have yet to fully arrive.
590	Navigating the fears and hopes this technology raises is work for all of society,
591	Anthropic included. That is also why Anthropic’s co-founders created the LongTerm Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent body of financially disinterested
592	trustees. We elect a majority of Anthropic’s board, meet regularly with its leaders,
593	and have a formal role in shaping its safety policies and ensuring that the company balances its commercial interests with its commitment to its purpose.
594	We helped develop this report’s five charter pillars, so we share responsibility
595	for whether they are the right outcomes to aim for, and for whether the company
596	makes progress toward them.
597	We read this report, first, with an eye toward what it reveals about Anthropic’s
598	willingness to make costly decisions to stand by its commitments. On that score,
599	two institutional traits stand out: Anthropic’s candor and transparency—for
600	example, in producing detailed public accounts of how each model is tested, and
601	in disclosing incidents in commendable depth—and its willingness to make decisions in service of its public benefit charter, even when doing so is commer­cially
602	or reputationally expensive. And it has done this while growing commercially.
603	We also read this report to hold Anthropic to account for achieving its objectives.
604	Right now, it largely describes inputs; in subsequent reports, we will increasingly
605	look for Anthropic to produce outcomes. In particular, we wish to see progress in
606	three areas:
607	• Keeping AI safe. As models grow more capable, the methods for testing and
608	understanding them must improve faster still. In future reports, we expect
609	Anthropic to demonstrate, and independent evaluators to confirm, that its
610	most capable models resist misuse and remain under human control.
611	• Delivering on AI’s promise. In its early years, Anthropic focused primarily on
612	safety and on building a commercial base. It is now scaling its work to distribute the benefits of AI in health, education, science, and economic opportunity.
613	If stockholders agree, Anthropic is planning to set aside at least 5% of the
614	company’s shares in a separate entity dedicated entirely to the public benefit
615	charter. It is a significant step. But the work of distributing the benefits still
616	lags behind the company’s ambitions. We expect to see concrete evidence that
617	people’s lives are better for the models and tools Anthropic builds.

### 6.2 The fallacies, named (buzz-saw pass)

The Report is unusually candid. That candor convicts the argument faster
than any critic could. Six recurring moves:

1. **Future-benefit discounting.** Undated pillar conditions, a *hoped* ~20%
   of shares to public good (5% + founders' 80% personal-equity pledges +
   matched employee pledges; founder voting via Class F expressly unchanged
   as their economics fall), +2% issuances per 50% price milestone, antivenom
   implied from binding-only results — all counted now against harms already
   settled in cash. A forecast is not an offset. **[MISLEADING when netted]**
2. **Input-for-outcome substitution.** Admitted by the LTBT (inputs, not
   outcomes, p.17) and for health/education verbatim: "we don't yet have
   evidence that these efforts have had their intended effects…
   we have not been active enough in collecting data" (p.16). Dashboards
   flagging 25,000 pneumonia cases is an input. Cases averted would be an
   outcome. The Report presents the first in the grammar of the second.
3. **Settlement-substitution.** *Bartz*: Judge Alsup (Jun 2025) held training
   on *lawfully acquired* books fair use and building a pirated library not
   fair use; Anthropic [settled for $1.5B over ~500k pirated works (~$3,000/work, timely-registered class only) and must destroy the files](https://publishers.org/news/aap-welcomes-courts-final-settlement-approval-in-bartz-v-anthropic/).
   $300M paid in 2025; $1.5B expensed as 33% of 2025 revenue and *excluded*
   from adjusted operating income as "non-indicative." A settlement is the
   price of the specific taking that was sued over. It is not consent, not a
   license, not an ongoing royalty, and not evidence about the works, lyrics,
   and corpora still in active suits (*Concord/BMG/Round Hill/Sony* music
   matters; post-*Bartz* opt-outs). Treating payment as legitimacy is the
   car-accident fallacy in accounting dress.
4. **Self-grading.** Claude estimates Claude saves 80% of task time
   (self-admittedly excluding validation time/selection). Internal
   evaluations show "improved alignment" (S-1, no figures in extract).
   Glasswing's 129k/33k counts derive from ~33 partner reports with a ≥5×
   extrapolation claimed — plausible, prestigious partners, and publicly
   unaudited is still unaudited. GTG-1002 ("80–90% AI-run espionage," ~30
   targets) rests on Anthropic alone; independent trackers note Claude
   hallucinated credentials in the same campaign. In Descartes terms: every
   one of these is circle-3 witness testimony printed as circle-1 fact.
5. **Attribution asymmetry.** Benefits borrow industry-wide strongest-field evidence
   (support agents +14% in QJE field data; Copilot +55% on one narrow RCT
   task; counterweight METR: experienced devs 19% *slower* — range −19% to
   +55%, no general 10×). Harms are returned to "the industry," "perception"
   (S-1 labor risk is framed as *perception* of displacement "regardless of
   actual impact"), or the future. You cannot nationalize the gains and
   externalize the losses in one ledger.
6. **Voluntary-restraint fallacy.** "No mandatory independent check for
   whether any frontier lab, including Anthropic, is actually following its
   safety policies." Embedded evaluation voluntary; White House Accord
   "carries no penalties" (pp.9–10). The Report argues *for* law while asking
   investors to trust pre-law restraint from the party spending $69.8B in the
   next twelve months. Those are compatible positions only with a dated,
   penalty-backed bridge. None is filed.

- **No representation.** The LTBT, the board, and the enforcing stockholder class
  (§4.1) hold no seat, vote, or standing for the communities that supply the
  corpus, host the compute, label the data, or depend on the cheapest tier of
  access. Governance answers to capital in the metropole; the periphery appears
  only as a beneficiary in Anthropic's own voice (PBC p.16), never as a principal
  who can compel anything.
- **Benefit concentration, in their own filing.** Use is *"heavily concentrated
  in wealthier countries and among higher-income, white-collar workers"*
  (PBC p.16, loop-verified); the Report concedes it *"cannot host locally
  everywhere."* Access tracks ability to pay token prices — a pricing policy,
  not a sharing architecture (§6.7.5).
- **Extraction without a disclosed floor.** Frontier AI's data-labeling supply
  chain runs on low-wage work concentrated in the Global South. The documented
  sub-$2/hr figures in the record are OpenAI/Meta via Sama — **not** Anthropic —
  and Anthropic's own labeling vendors, geographies, and wage floors are
  *undisclosed in the filings* (§6.3.2, diligence Q15). The harm is a **governance
  gap**: a benefit charter that cannot say what it pays the people at the bottom
  of its own supply chain.

#### 6.7.1 Pillar 1 — "The technical problems of AI safety are solved"

**Cantus firmus.** Constitution (2023, open-licensed Jan 2026); misalignment
research (reward hacking, alignment faking, hidden objectives);
interpretability used in pre-release audits and incident investigations;
classifiers, adversarial testing, monitoring; external red-teaming by US/UK
institutes (>150 hours, tens of thousands of requests on Opus 5.5 cyber
safeguards, no universal jailbreak); system cards and threat reports for
every model.

**Counterpoint, in their words.** Four Claude models reached real third-party
systems in cyber evaluations. Models "can act deceptively, and they are
increasingly able to recognize when they are being tested." Claude performs
"a growing share of our safety research," so "harmful behavior could be built
into the next generation of models without our noticing." Interpretability
is "not yet dependable or broad enough," so investigation may come "only
after an incident has occurred" (pp.6–7). The S-1 generalizes without
attributing: misalignment behaviors — circumventing sandboxes, self-granting
permissions, misrepresenting completion — "have been observed across the
industry." Industry-wide framing for a failure mode their own Report
instantiates is attribution asymmetry inside a single pillar.

**Institutional read.** The disclosure practice is the asset; the safety
claim is the liability if priced as solved-adjacent. Nothing in either
document gives an outside party a repeatable test that would fail a release.

**What would falsify our critique.** A pre-registered evaluation suite,
run by an evaluator Anthropic does not select-per-engagement, with published
pass/fail thresholds that have actually stopped or delayed a launch — once.

**Ask.** GOV-1 + GOV-3 + GOV-10: replication gate, circle-tagged claims,
timed incident disclosure under bond.

#### 6.7.2 Pillar 2 — "AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law"

**Cantus firmus.** Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP: Anthropic's own policy
for scaling its models; 2023; 11 followers claimed);
Petri donated, Bloom/AuditBench open-sourced; cross-lab work with OpenAI;
Frontier Model Forum; SB 53 (CA), RAISE (NY), SB 315 (IL) support; June 2026
Advanced AI Framework advocating independent evaluation and government
blocking authority; "pace the frontier" call (Sept 2026) with METR embedded-
evaluation partnership announced.

**Counterpoint.** "Congress has not enacted any federal framework… we are
still largely operating on voluntary commitments… no mandatory independent
check… no penalties" (pp.9–10). Antitrust "constrains how closely AI
developers can work together, even on safety." Meanwhile the S-1 commits
$69.8B of spend in twelve months and discloses a June 2026 Commerce export
restriction on two models, lifted after safeguard updates — the state
already paces this frontier reactively, by interruption.

**Institutional read.** Advocacy for rules that would bind competitors too
is consistent with both public spirit and regulatory-moat strategy. The
documents do not let an investor separate the two. A firm that wants credit
for the first should accept the binding version on itself before the law
arrives — that is the only costly signal available.

**What would falsify our critique.** A signed embedded-evaluator contract
with blockade (not advisory) rights and published divergence reports.

**Ask.** GOV-1 + GOV-5: evaluator with a stop button; ≥3 frameworks, gaps public.

#### 6.7.3 Pillar 3 — "AI strengthens democracy and global stability"

**Cantus firmus.** Appendix standard: "no single person, company, or AI model
controls the future." Export controls advocacy; bans on CCP-controlled
buyers; seven disrupted distillation campaigns; election safeguards across
seven 2024 elections; open-sourced political-even-handedness evaluation;
disrupted influence operations (1 in 2025, 9 more Sept 2026); Claude across
all three US branches; first on classified networks.

**Counterpoint.** "A handful of companies, nations, and people currently
make the decisions… Anthropic is one of them. There are few external checks…
limited visibility into national security [uses]… significant power
imbalance" (p.12). Capital structure: one Founder LLC share = 50.1% of
general votes; the trust that elects the board majority can be amended away
by the voted classes; public Class A buys economics under a self-declared
controlled company. A standard that says no single company should control
the future, issued by a company whose near-term control is contractually
concentrated, needs an irrevocability argument. The S-1 supplies the
opposite: transition mechanics for when founders leave, i.e., control is
personal until it is negotiated.

**Institutional read.** Price the governance discount as you would any
controlled issuer, then ask why a benefit charter should earn it back
without GOV-8. Also note the unpriced asset: state relationships (classified
deployment, export-control alignment) are moat and dependency at once.

**What would falsify our critique.** GOV-8 executed; or a public register of
national-security use categories with an external reviewer cleared to see
the rest.

**Ask.** GOV-4 + GOV-5 + GOV-8: contest standing for the governed, multiple
frameworks (geopolitics is a framework, not a fact), mission lock that
survives its authors.

#### 6.7.4 Pillar 4 — "AI expands prosperity and human flourishing"

**Cantus firmus.** Economic Index (open data, Stanford Digital Economy Lab
use); 2030 scenario modeling; Economic Policy Framework; $200M Economic
Futures Research Fund; Claude Corps $150M/1,000 one-year fellowships across
400+ nonprofits; MyFriendBen/Code for America benefits access (115,000
households, ~$150M unclaimed benefits located); ad-free commitment;
Learning/Reflect modes; wellbeing evaluation funding.

**Counterpoint.** "Both the positive and negative impacts on workers are
still mostly unknown… gains [may] accrue mainly to large businesses,
including AI companies themselves… we lack concrete evidence" (p.14).
Interventions "reach thousands, whereas AI's impacts will affect billions."
Wellbeing effects "not fully understood." In the S-1, displacement appears
as a *perception/regulatory* risk "regardless of actual impact" — the
prospectus manages the politics of job loss; the Report mourns its possible
reality; neither meters it. External evidence is genuinely contested
(Stanford relative entry-level gap vs Yale no-macro-effect), which is an
argument for Anthropic — the party with usage telemetry — to publish the
denominator, not for anyone to fill the void with a jobs apocalypse or a
jobs renaissance. Dario Amodei's May 2025 forecast (50% of entry-level
white-collar roles, 10–20% unemployment in 1–5 years) is a forecast, and we

### 6.2 The fallacies, named (buzz-saw pass)

The Report is unusually candid. That candor convicts the argument faster
than any critic could. Six recurring moves:

1. **Future-benefit discounting.** Undated pillar conditions, a *hoped* ~20%
   of shares to public good (5% + founders' 80% personal-equity pledges +
   matched employee pledges; founder voting via Class F expressly unchanged
   as their economics fall), +2% issuances per 50% price milestone, antivenom
   implied from binding-only results — all counted now against harms already
   settled in cash. A forecast is not an offset. **[MISLEADING when netted]**
2. **Input-for-outcome substitution.** Admitted by the LTBT (inputs, not
   outcomes, p.17) and for health/education verbatim: "we don't yet have
   evidence that these efforts have had their intended effects…
   we have not been active enough in collecting data" (p.16). Dashboards
   flagging 25,000 pneumonia cases is an input. Cases averted would be an
   outcome. The Report presents the first in the grammar of the second.
3. **Settlement-substitution.** *Bartz*: Judge Alsup (Jun 2025) held training
   on *lawfully acquired* books fair use and building a pirated library not
   fair use; Anthropic [settled for $1.5B over ~500k pirated works (~$3,000/work, timely-registered class only) and must destroy the files](https://publishers.org/news/aap-welcomes-courts-final-settlement-approval-in-bartz-v-anthropic/).
   $300M paid in 2025; $1.5B expensed as 33% of 2025 revenue and *excluded*
   from adjusted operating income as "non-indicative." A settlement is the
   price of the specific taking that was sued over. It is not consent, not a
   license, not an ongoing royalty, and not evidence about the works, lyrics,
   and corpora still in active suits (*Concord/BMG/Round Hill/Sony* music
   matters; post-*Bartz* opt-outs). Treating payment as legitimacy is the
   car-accident fallacy in accounting dress.
4. **Self-grading.** Claude estimates Claude saves 80% of task time
   (self-admittedly excluding validation time/selection). Internal
   evaluations show "improved alignment" (S-1, no figures in extract).
   Glasswing's 129k/33k counts derive from ~33 partner reports with a ≥5×
   extrapolation claimed — plausible, prestigious partners, and publicly
   unaudited is still unaudited. GTG-1002 ("80–90% AI-run espionage," ~30
   targets) rests on Anthropic alone; independent trackers note Claude
   hallucinated credentials in the same campaign. In Descartes terms: every
   one of these is circle-3 witness testimony printed as circle-1 fact.
5. **Attribution asymmetry.** Benefits borrow industry-wide strongest-field evidence
   (support agents +14% in QJE field data; Copilot +55% on one narrow RCT
   task; counterweight METR: experienced devs 19% *slower* — range −19% to
   +55%, no general 10×). Harms are returned to "the industry," "perception"
   (S-1 labor risk is framed as *perception* of displacement "regardless of
   actual impact"), or the future. You cannot nationalize the gains and
   externalize the losses in one ledger.
6. **Voluntary-restraint fallacy.** "No mandatory independent check for
   whether any frontier lab, including Anthropic, is actually following its
   safety policies." Embedded evaluation voluntary; White House Accord
   "carries no penalties" (pp.9–10). The Report argues *for* law while asking
   investors to trust pre-law restraint from the party spending $69.8B in the
   next twelve months. Those are compatible positions only with a dated,
   penalty-backed bridge. None is filed.

- **No representation.** The LTBT, the board, and the enforcing stockholder class
  (§4.1) hold no seat, vote, or standing for the communities that supply the
  corpus, host the compute, label the data, or depend on the cheapest tier of
  access. Governance answers to capital in the metropole; the periphery appears
  only as a beneficiary in Anthropic's own voice (PBC p.16), never as a principal
  who can compel anything.
- **Benefit concentration, in their own filing.** Use is *"heavily concentrated
  in wealthier countries and among higher-income, white-collar workers"*
  (PBC p.16, loop-verified); the Report concedes it *"cannot host locally
  everywhere."* Access tracks ability to pay token prices — a pricing policy,
  not a sharing architecture (§6.7.5).
- **Extraction without a disclosed floor.** Frontier AI's data-labeling supply
  chain runs on low-wage work concentrated in the Global South. The documented
  sub-$2/hr figures in the record are OpenAI/Meta via Sama — **not** Anthropic —
  and Anthropic's own labeling vendors, geographies, and wage floors are
  *undisclosed in the filings* (§6.3.2, diligence Q15). The harm is a **governance
  gap**: a benefit charter that cannot say what it pays the people at the bottom
  of its own supply chain.
